In software development, pinpointing where a specific concept resides within a codebase is a crucial task. Although developers can manually locate these concepts, the process is time-consuming and error-prone. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach leveraging crowdsourced knowledge to identify concept locations. Our method utilizes crowd-sourced information to generate a conceptual map, which is then used to generate a list of potential concept locations. We evaluated our approach using 10 open-source projects, achieving an average F-measure of 0.61 for concept location.

A block-diagonal preconditioner is suggested to enhance the convergence of an iterative solver for complex systems. This system comprises multiple interconnected nonlinear equations, each having a distinct physical meaning. By approximating the coupling between these equations, a block-diagonal preconditioner can be constructed, consisting of the diagonal elements of the Jacobian matrix. This approach is particularly useful when the individual equation solvers are well-established and efficient. Moreover, it can be easily implemented in parallel environments, making it a practical solution for large-scale simulations. This paper presents a detailed description of the implementation of the block-diagonal preconditioner in the context of the OpenFOAM solver, along with its application to the simulation of the thermal behavior of a lithium-ion battery.

Recent breakthroughs in abstractive dialogue summarization have been achieved, 
yet the underlying models often lack transparency in how they interpret the dialogue. 
To address this limitation, our study introduces a novel approach that leverages 
discourse relations to enhance the interpretability of abstractive dialogue summarization. 
By integrating these relations into the summarization process, our model can explicitly 
highlight the connections between the generated summary and the original dialogue. 
Our proposed framework is demonstrated through an end-to-end model that incorporates 
discourse relations into the summarization process, and our experimental results show 
that our approach outperforms existing models in both automated and human evaluations.

This paper demonstrates that deep learning methods can be used to accurately calculate the Doppler broadening of cross-sections, significantly reducing computation time. The model is trained using data from the NJOY code and is able to predict cross-sections for various temperatures and elements, achieving high accuracy. The model is also shown to be effective in nuclear applications, particularly in modeling temperature-dependent effects.

This paper develops two methods for constructing $(n+1)$-pre-Lie algebras from $n$-pre-Lie algebras. It then examines coalgebras dual to non-associative algebras and offers a method for creating novel $(n+1)$-pre-Lie algebras from $n$-pre-Lie algebras using the dualization process. Furthermore, the study identifies novel examples of $(n+1)$-pre-Lie algebras from the well-known Lie algebras and pre-Lie algebras.

This research focuses on the efficient allocation of resources for users with diverse quality-of-service requirements in a multi-user wireless system. A new approach is introduced to address this issue, which involves jointly optimizing power allocation and user scheduling to meet the specific needs of each user. The approach is divided into two stages: first, a power allocation strategy is developed to minimize the energy usage of each user while meeting their quality-of-service requirements. Next, a user scheduling algorithm is proposed to select the most suitable users for transmission based on their individual power allocation results. The approach is shown to be effective in reducing the energy usage of each user while maintaining their quality-of-service requirements. A numerical study is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed scheme, which demonstrates that it can achieve a significant improvement in the quality-of-service requirements of real-time users compared to a simple power allocation strategy.

We establish that applying translations along the real axis to an entire function yields an approximate reproduction of that function, either pointwise or uniformly on any compact domain, with the approximation being a function of the number of iterations applied.

The behavior of disordered materials under deformation is heavily influenced by their internal structure, which can be manipulated to achieve desired material properties. To understand the connection between structure and material performance, we developed a computational model that simulates the deformation of disordered materials. By using this model, we were able to create materials with different structures and test their response to shear forces. We found that the characteristics of the material's internal structure, such as the arrangement of particles and the distribution of distances between them, have a significant impact on the material's rheological properties. We were able to use this information to develop a method for predicting the material's behavior under different conditions. Our results show that it is possible to design materials with tailored properties by manipulating their internal structure.

Continuous learning in object detection is crucial for real-world applications like robotics and self-driving cars, where robots and vehicles constantly encounter unfamiliar objects. However, existing continual learning methods for object detection often neglect the importance of retaining previously seen data, leading to a significant loss of information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Re-Play with Memory-Augmented Neural Networks (RP-MANN), which leverages the capabilities of memory-augmented neural networks to retain and integrate past experiences. By employing a memory-augmented re-sampling strategy, RP-MANN can effectively select relevant past experiences, thereby enhancing the performance of continual learning in object detection. Our experimental results demonstrate that RP-MANN outperforms existing methods in object detection tasks, achieving superior performance on the COCO dataset.

We examine the influence of electromagnetic fields on the production of quark-antiquark pairs in heavy-ion collisions using quantum kinetic theory. Our analysis reveals that the fields can significantly boost quark-antiquark production when the product of the inverse electromagnetic field strength and the collision system size exceeds a certain threshold. This threshold is crucial for understanding the role of electromagnetic fields in heavy-ion collisions. Our findings also show that the fields can lead to a substantial increase in the production of light quark-antiquark pairs, particularly for electrons and muons. This enhancement is more pronounced in the transverse momentum range of 0.5-1.0 GeV/c, where the electromagnetic fields dominate the production of these leptons. Our results also indicate that the electromagnetic fields can have a significant impact on the production of strange and charm quarks, particularly in the transverse momentum range of 0.5-2 GeV/c. This enhancement is more pronounced in the transverse momentum range of 0.5-2 GeV/c, where the electromagnetic fields dominate the production of these quarks. Our findings have important implications for the understanding of heavy-ion collisions and the role of electromagnetic fields in these events.

Achieving generalization in computer vision is a pressing challenge, particularly in the context of object detection. To address this, we introduce DivCAM, a large-scale dataset comprising over 100,000 images across 10 domains, designed to facilitate domain generalization. DivCAM is a composite dataset that aggregates images from diverse sources, including COCO, Open Images, and various other datasets, thereby providing a rich and varied training environment. To aid in the development of robust neural networks, we provide DivCAM with detailed metadata and a powerful tool, DivCAM Explorer, which enables users to analyze domain characteristics and inter-domain relationships. By leveraging DivCAM and its accompanying resources, we aim to foster the development of more effective and adaptable computer vision models.

This paper explores the potential of an innovative, platform-agnostic blockchain to enhance and optimize the behavior of Internet infrastructure by improving its agent models. By leveraging a custom, custom-built blockchain, we enable the creation of a decentralized, collaborative ecosystem where diverse participants can interact and exchange information securely. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this blockchain by applying it to a real-world scenario: a decentralized Domain Name System (DNS) that prioritizes security and efficiency. Our implementation utilizes a combination of blockchain technology and advanced data structures to achieve efficient consensus and secure communication. Through a comprehensive analysis of the system's performance, we validate its reliability and scalability, paving the way for further exploration of blockchain-based solutions in other Internet infrastructure applications.

We investigated single-field exponential and polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models in supergravity, specifically the $\alpha$-attractor models with a potential $V(\phi)$, where $\phi$ is a real field. We used the Planck 2018 data to determine the best-fit parameters for these models. We found that both models are consistent with the data, with the exponential model providing a slightly better fit than the polynomial one. The $\alpha$-attractor models with $\alpha=0.0234$ for the exponential case and $\alpha=0.0235$ for the polynomial case are the best-fit models. We also found that the exponential model with a non-zero $\alpha$ is a more natural choice than the polynomial one.

The optimization of AI pipelines has become a critical area of focus, with research indicating that significant performance gains can be achieved through various optimization techniques. Despite the potential for substantial improvements, the vast number of possible configurations and the complexity of the optimization process make it challenging to identify the most effective optimizations for a given pipeline. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a graph-based representation of AI pipelines to enable the optimization process to be guided by a reinforcement learning agent. By training our agent on a large dataset of real-world AI pipelines, we demonstrate that it can successfully identify the most effective optimizations for new pipelines, resulting in a 1.2x improvement in performance compared to the state-of-the-art. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the optimization process, highlighting the key optimizations that lead to the most significant performance gains.

Researchers often use the Bayes Factor, along with high density intervals and region of practical equivalence, to assess equivalence in studies. However, the Bayes Factor's variability can be unpredictable, leading to questions about its reliability. To investigate this, researchers compared the Bayes Factor to the frequentist equivalence test and found that the Bayes Factor has a lower type 2 error rate when compared to other methods. Nevertheless, they found that the Bayes Factor has a higher median power compared to frequentist equivalence tests. To address this, researchers introduced a new method called the frequentist Bayes Factor test, which adjusts the Bayes Factor's results to match the frequentist test's characteristics. The frequentist Bayes Factor test showed a significant improvement in the Bayes Factor test, with a 20% increase in median power and a 50% decrease in variability. The results suggest that the Bayes Factor test may be a useful alternative to the frequentist equivalence test, particularly in situations where the Bayes Factor's variability is a concern.

In digital semantic communication, the goal is to convey the underlying meaning of a received image by training a receiver to extract it from the transmitted image. This paper explores the effectiveness of adversarial training in enhancing image quality at the receiver end. We introduce a new training approach that utilizes the receiver as the encoder and the transmitter as the generator, allowing us to examine the impact of adversarial training on the quality of received images. We also analyze the mathematical properties of this training method and its implications for the performance of the SC system. Furthermore, we extend the concept of adversarial training to scenarios with channel noise, demonstrating that adversarial training can significantly improve the quality of received images in such scenarios.

In the realm of data processing, the concept of skew has been extensively studied, but the field of data skew management has been somewhat underdeveloped, particularly in relation to the use of abstractions. This paper aims to bridge this gap by exploring the potential of language-based techniques in addressing data skew. We examine the effectiveness of using a language-based approach to manage skew, focusing on the Reshape framework, which allows users to express data skew mitigation strategies through syntactic transformations. We demonstrate the benefits of Reshape by applying it to a real-world problem, showcasing its ability to automatically detect and rectify data skew in a MapReduce program. We also discuss the potential of Reshape as a framework for managing skew in other programming models and explore its implications for future research in this area.

We investigate how much information is lost when transitioning from a comonad or an adjunction $L \dashrightarrow R$ to a modal interior operator, and we find that the information loss can be measured using the difference between the image of the unit and the identity on an object. This difference can be expressed as a specific subobject of the identity, which we call the "loss." We demonstrate that the information loss can be interpreted as a measure of the inefficiency of the modal interior operator, and we show that it can be used to quantify the efficiency of the modal interior operator in terms of the information loss it introduces. We also establish that the information loss can be used to compare the efficiency of different modal interior operators, and we show that the information loss can be used to quantify the efficiency of a modal interior operator in terms of the information loss it introduces.

A new Bayesian model for network autoregression is introduced, which takes into account the dynamic nature of network evolution. Building on the concept of the Chinese restaurant process, this approach provides a visual framework for incorporating prior knowledge about network growth. This novel framework enables the incorporation of prior beliefs about network growth rates and offers a visual aid for model diagnostics. The resulting model offers a more comprehensive statistical analysis, which is demonstrated through its application to real-world data, showcasing its ability to uncover temporal patterns and relationships that are not apparent in static network analysis.

A pioneering dataset called SciFact is introduced, designed to assess the credibility of scientific statements by utilizing an enhanced fact-checking framework. Comprising 45,000 meticulously verified scientific claims, this dataset is significantly larger than its predecessors and boasts a balanced distribution of factual and factual claims. To facilitate in-depth analysis, SciFact incorporates a comprehensive set of 10 fine-grained labels that capture the nuances of scientific reasoning. To support the assessment process, SciFact provides a rich array of supporting and contradicting evidence, including citations and knowledge graph connections. To aid in the evaluation of SciFact, 27 state-of-the-art fact-checking models were tested, with their performance analyzed in detail. The results reveal that no model excelled in all categories, underscoring the need for models that can leverage diverse knowledge sources and incorporate both textual and structured information. The SciFact benchmark is made publicly available to foster advancements in scientific claim verification research.

A novel, unsupervised deep learning approach is presented for segmenting the eye in color fundus photography. The method, which requires no manual labeling, is effective in both normal and abnormal scans. The approach first identifies the eye's inner and outer boundaries, then uses a pre-trained model to segment the eye's internal structures. The model's weights are adjusted using the identified boundaries, and it is trained to recognize the eye's retina, vessels, and other features. The method's performance is evaluated using two datasets, and it is shown to accurately segment the eye in both normal and abnormal scans. The results demonstrate that the method can accurately identify the eye's internal structures, and it is robust to variations in image quality.

Cognitive modeling often employs temporal dynamics analysis to uncover underlying mechanisms, but this approach is frequently hindered by the unrealistic assumption that model parameters remain constant over time. This assumption can lead to biased and inaccurate model outcomes, as it disregards the inherent variability in parameters. This research presents a novel method for addressing this issue by incorporating a latent process that accounts for parameter variability over time. This approach is demonstrated through its application to a temporal decision-making model, where the decision threshold is modeled as a time-varying parameter. By using this method, we can accurately capture the temporal dynamics of parameters and obtain more reliable model outcomes.

We introduce a novel Mersenne compositeness criterion and demonstrate several cases of its application. Additionally, we present an efficient method for identifying pseudoprimes that satisfy this criterion. This criterion is founded on a novel congruence relation modulating the square of an algebraic integer within a specific field, with the exact nature of this congruence contingent upon the primality or compositeness of a given Mersenne number.

The Boltzmann equation's behavior is investigated under the combined effects of high dispersion and high dissipation. This analysis is relevant to systems exhibiting weak hydrodynamic interactions, such as those in plasmas and neutron star atmospheres. In these cases, the Boltzmann equation's collision term is simplified through the combined effects of dispersive dominance and high dissipation. This leads to a novel hydrodynamic framework that incorporates the effects of high dissipation. This framework is compared to the traditional Chapman-Enskog expansion, which neglects the effects of high dissipation. It is demonstrated that the novel framework provides a more accurate description of systems exhibiting high dissipation, particularly in systems with small Knudsen numbers. This is achieved by incorporating the effects of high dissipation into the hydrodynamic equations, which leads to the emergence of new terms that are not present in the traditional Chapman-Enskog expansion. These new terms are shown to be essential for accurately describing systems exhibiting high dissipation.

Our study of 12 CO and 13 CO emission from extreme starburst galaxies at redshifts of 0.5 to 1.5, using the ALMA telescope, reveals that the ratios of CO line emissions are significantly influenced by low-density gas. This is evident in the ratios of CO 12/13, which are found to be 10-20 times higher than in the Milky Way, and the ratios of CO 4/3, which are 2-3 times higher. These findings suggest that the extreme starburst galaxies are experiencing low-density gas conditions, which could be due to the presence of molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. Furthermore, our analysis of the relationship between CO emission and star formation rate shows that the latter is a better indicator of the former than the CO 13 emission. These results have important implications for understanding the role of low-density gas in extreme starburst galaxies.

To enhance the accuracy of annotations, we suggest that annotators be informed about the discrepancies in their evaluations compared to others, which can be achieved by leveraging the data from the annotation process itself. This approach is demonstrated to be effective in improving inter-annotator agreement, particularly in the context of the Transcribed Spoken Document Corpus, where we utilize the annotation data to provide annotators with feedback on the inconsistencies in their assessments.

The dispersal of circumstellar discs is a crucial step in the development of planetary systems, but the underlying mechanisms driving this process remain unclear. A recent study of 100 young stars in the Taurus-Auriga-Auriga-Aries complex, which are approximately 1-10 million years old, has shed new light on this phenomenon. By analyzing the stellar masses and inner-disc lifetimes of these young stars, researchers found a strong correlation between the two, which suggests that the dispersal of discs is closely tied to the mass of the star. A detailed analysis of the relationship between the mass of the star and the lifetime of its inner disc revealed a power-law relationship, which is consistent with the predictions of the viscous dissipation model. A comparison of the results with previous studies of similar young stars revealed a consistent pattern, which suggests that the dispersal of discs is a universal phenomenon that occurs across a wide range of ages and masses. A statistical analysis of the results revealed that the dispersal of discs is a gradual process that occurs over a period of several million years, which is consistent with the predictions of the viscous dissipation model. A comparison of the results with previous studies of similar young stars revealed a consistent pattern, which suggests that the dispersal of discs is a universal phenomenon that occurs across a wide range of ages and masses.

A new approach to solving the 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations is presented, utilizing a spectral method with adjustable coefficients to control numerical dissipation. By modifying these coefficients, high-frequency regions can be effectively damped, while lower-frequency regions remain unaffected. This technique is particularly beneficial for simulating turbulent flows, where it can be used to model subgrid-scale interactions. By adjusting the dissipation factor, the method can be used to simulate both fully resolved and large-eddy simulations. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness in accurately simulating turbulent flows, including forced turbulence and decaying turbulence.

The behavior of a polaron in a double-well potential is studied using a three-component Gross-Pitaevskii equation. This equation models a system consisting of a Bose gas and a single impurity atom, with the latter experiencing both attraction and repulsion forces. We analyze the effects of the relative repulsion of the Bose gas on the polaron's double-well condensate properties, including its energy, wave function, and the double-well energy gap. We find that the repulsion of the Bose gas significantly influences the residue behaviors of the polaron, including the emergence of multiple local minima in the double-well condensate properties.

A hurricane relief supply chain is modeled using a Markov chain framework to analyze the prepositioning of relief items in warehouses. The optimal inventory levels for each location are determined by considering the hurricane risk and demand uncertainty, and the model's performance is evaluated through the analysis of the hurricane activity in the Gulf Coast region. The prepositioning strategy is then adapted to scenarios where hurricane forecasts are available, and the model's effectiveness is demonstrated through the application of the hurricane risk model to real-world data from Florida.

In the context of pulsar timing arrays, the approximate analytic expressions for the overlap reduction function and its Fourier transform are found to be highly accurate, with a maximum error of 0.5%. The reliability of these expressions is demonstrated by their compatibility with other analytical methods and numerical simulations. The expressions' simplicity makes them suitable for use in Bayesian analyses, with the ability to provide accurate results in the presence of Gaussian noise.

In Bayesian multi-agent games, we investigate the conditions under which multiple equilibria can be successfully coordinated, given that agents have limited cognitive capabilities. Our approach involves categorizing games into two types: those where coordination is impossible and those where it is feasible. For the latter, we establish a systematic method to identify the equilibria that agents can converge upon, even when they have restricted decision-making abilities. Our findings are applied to a specific model of a coordination game, the "battle of the sexes," to illustrate the implications of our analysis.

A novel method of THz spectroscopy has been developed for analyzing transparent liquids, allowing for the measurement of their optical properties. This method combines a special THz waveguide with a microfluidic channel, enabling the precise control of the THz wave's interaction with the liquid, and thus the determination of its dielectric properties. As the THz wave's interaction length can be adjusted by modifying the channel's dimensions, this technique offers the potential for highly accurate measurements of thin liquid films. This method has been successfully applied to measure the dielectric properties of water at various temperatures, and the results show good agreement with existing data. Moreover, this technique has the potential to be used for the analysis of other liquids, and the ability to measure the THz wave's interaction with the liquid at various angles and polarizations makes it a versatile tool for the study of liquid properties.

The spread of infectious diseases is influenced by a multitude of factors, including environmental conditions and human behavior. This research introduces a predictive model for disease transmission risk that incorporates multiple variables, using a deep learning approach. The model, a deep neural network, takes into account the interplay between various factors, such as weather patterns, population mobility, and social interactions, to forecast the risk of outbreaks in specific regions. By analyzing data from the COVID-19 pandemic, our model demonstrated its ability to accurately predict disease transmission, outperforming existing methods. This research highlights the potential of deep learning in understanding and predicting infectious disease outbreaks, paving the way for more effective public health interventions.

A novel multi-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method is developed to simulate high-velocity, high-density ratio collisions between different materials. The approach combines a multi-resolution framework with a particle-based method to handle large-scale problems. The proposed method uses a multi-phase model to address voids and phase separation issues, and a new equation of state is implemented to simulate high-pressure conditions. The framework also includes a novel method for handling large-scale problems by using a multi-resolution approach. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulations of high-velocity impacts, including the impact of a solid projectile on a target, and the impact of a liquid projectile on a target. The results show that the method accurately captures the complex physics of high-velocity, high-density ratio collisions, and can be used to simulate a wide range of applications, including astrophysical phenomena and industrial processes.

The topological states of matter are classified by their boundary between the trivial and topological phases. Nodal lines, a unique form of topology, are characterized by their stability and robust degeneracy, but their behavior in the presence of perturbations is not well understood. Our research reveals that nodal lines can be divided into two distinct categories: those that are stable and those that are not. We discovered that the stability of nodal lines is determined by the presence of certain symmetries, specifically those that are not present in the standard crystal symmetries. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of nodal lines and their potential applications in the development of new materials with unique properties.

To prepare for the high-luminosity experiments at the LHC, it's essential to develop efficient and reliable event generator software. This article presents the initial findings of a simulation study conducted to evaluate the performance of the PYTHIA 8 Monte Carlo event generator under the demanding conditions of high-luminosity experiments. The study focuses on the challenges of processing events at a high rate of 10^35 luminosity, where events are generated at a high frequency, and the computational resources are heavily strained. The research investigates the performance of PYTHIA 8 in terms of CPU efficiency, memory usage, and the accuracy of the generated events, and provides recommendations for optimizing the software to meet the needs of future experiments.

This paper examines the interconnection between Sierpinski's concept of invariant means and mean-type mappings. Properties of both are defined in terms of their respective invariants. A class of mean-type mappings is introduced, and a mapping is categorized based on its properties in relation to its Sierpi\'nski mean. A Sierpi\'nski mean is defined as the unique fixed point of a mean-type mapping, which enables the classification of an arbitrary mean-type mapping based on its Sierpi\'nski mean.

Our research into the distribution of molecular gas in the outer Galaxy, using CO(1-0) data from the APEX survey, reveals a distinct pattern compared to the distribution of HI gas. The molecular gas is more concentrated towards the center, with a significant decline in its presence beyond a certain radius. This phenomenon is attributed to the collapse of gas clouds and the formation of new stars. The evidence for this process is supported by the presence of young stars and the detection of molecular outflows in the outer Galaxy. The findings suggest that the outer Galaxy is a site of active star formation, with the collapse of gas clouds and the formation of new stars playing a crucial role.

The consumer choice game is utilized to analyze wage redistribution. We introduce a new approach to calibrate the consumer choice game by leveraging aggregate consumption data, thereby enabling the estimation of wage distributions.

Active matter's self-propulsion is crucial in understanding various biological and nonbiological systems. A particular type of active matter, known as active glasses, is characterized by jammed states and a lack of movement. A recent study has found that active glasses can be influenced by a specific type of interaction, which causes particles to align. This interaction can significantly affect the behavior of active glasses, causing them to undergo a transition from a jammed state to a fluid state. A theoretical model has been developed to explain this transition, which is based on the idea that particles can be influenced by their surroundings. This model has been shown to accurately describe the behavior of active glasses, including the way in which they can become fluidized. A key finding of this study is that active glasses can be influenced by their surroundings, which can cause them to undergo a transition from a jammed state to a fluid state. This model has been shown to be a useful tool for understanding the behavior of active glasses, and it may have applications in a variety of fields, including materials science and biology.

Theoretical predictions for the decay rates of the doubly charmed baryon $\Lambda_{cc}$ into a $B_c$ meson and a lepton are made using the heavy-quark effective theory. The predicted branching ratios for the $\tau$ and $e$ decay modes are found to be $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ and $4.0 \times 10^{-6}$ respectively. The decay ratio of the $\tau$ mode to the $e$ mode is found to be larger than one, suggesting that lepton flavor plays a significant role in the semileptonic decays of the doubly charmed baryon. The decay rates of the $\tau$ and $e$ modes are also found to be within the range of the experimentally accessible limits.

In our research, we propose a novel game called Observer-Capture where two players, the Observer and the Locator, engage in a game of hide-and-seek on a graph. The Observer attempts to evade detection by moving to a hidden vertex, while the Locator tries to identify the Observer's chosen location. We examine the strategies employed by both players, particularly focusing on the Locator's ability to successfully locate the Observer within a limited number of queries. We developed a model called the Observer-bot that utilizes the Locator's available information to determine the Observer's chosen location. Our experiments show that the Observer-bot achieves a success rate of 85.5%, significantly higher than humans, who achieve a success rate of only 52.6%. We also investigate the strategies employed by the Observer and the Locator, including the use of randomization and the identification of the Locator's optimal strategy. We find that the Observer can significantly improve their success rate by using a randomized strategy, particularly when the graph is large. Our results suggest that the use of randomization is a key factor in the Observer's success.

In the field of machinery monitoring, selecting the most relevant frequency bands is a crucial step, but current methods often rely on arbitrary thresholds or fixed frequency ranges. This research introduces a novel approach to frequency band selection, which utilizes a new metric called the Band Relevance Factor (BRF). By analyzing the BRF, the most pertinent frequency bands can be identified, thereby enhancing the efficiency of signal processing and reducing computational costs. The proposed method was tested using data from a faulty bearing, which demonstrated its effectiveness in isolating the most relevant frequency bands.

The superconducting properties of the materials CaPtSi3 and CaIrSi3 have been studied using the technique of muon spin rotation/relaxation/precession. The results indicate that CaPtSi3 has a significantly longer superconducting coherence length, approximately 100 nm, compared to CaIrSi3 at 10 nm. This substantial difference in coherence length is attributed to the distinct electronic properties of the materials, with CaPtSi3 having a smaller density of states at the Fermi level and a higher Fermi velocity. The longer coherence length in CaPtSi3 is believed to be related to its smaller Fermi surface, which is characterized by a single hole pocket, whereas CaIrSi3 has a more complex Fermi surface with both electron and hole pockets. The results of this study provide insight into the electronic properties of these materials and may contribute to a better understanding of their superconducting behavior.

The Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation is a crucial component in solving the optimal control problem, but its solution is hindered by the curse of dimensionality, which affects traditional numerical methods. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes deep learning to approximate the value function, and we prove that this method can achieve the same level of accuracy as traditional numerical schemes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to a wide range of problems, including those with high dimensions, and we provide numerical results that support our theoretical findings.

Recent advancements in quantum computing have opened up new possibilities for enhancing supervised classification techniques. This paper introduces a quantum neural network that leverages the quantum circuit model, incorporating the quantum channel's unitary operator to optimize the neural network. The proposed quantum neural network is capable of handling a wide range of tasks, including regression, binary classification, and multi-class classification. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the quantum neural network can outperform its classical counterpart in specific scenarios. Experimentally, we utilize IBM's cloud-based quantum computers to evaluate the performance of the quantum neural network in regression, binary classification, and multi-class classification tasks. The results show that the quantum neural network achieves competitive performance with classical neural networks, particularly in regression and binary classification tasks.

The increasing presence of distributed energy resources in electric power systems is driving the need for more granular and efficient control strategies. This is where multi-layered energy modeling comes into play, offering a detailed representation of the grid and its control capabilities. This paper introduces a novel approach to multi-layered modeling, which leverages the strengths of both detailed and reduced-order models. This hybrid modeling framework is then utilized to develop a two-tiered optimization framework for grid integration of distributed energy resources. This framework is demonstrated through a case study involving the integration of a distributed energy system into a transmission network, showcasing how the two-tiered optimization framework can effectively utilize both detailed and reduced-order models to achieve optimal results.

This paper delves into the potential of deep learning to uncover the underlying characteristics of percolation states in a binary mixture. By training a neural network on a dataset of binary mixtures, it can accurately predict the percolation state of a given system. Furthermore, it can extract key features such as density and correlation length from the given input. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning in identifying percolation states and extracting percolation characteristics from a given binary mixture image.

A reliable and non-invasive method for measuring temperature in large reactors is the proton resonance frequency shift technique. This method utilizes the temperature-dependent change in resonance frequency of protons to determine the reactor's temperature. By combining this frequency shift with a chemical shift reference, the method can accurately measure temperatures in the range of 20-300 K. A new approach to enhance the method's precision and efficiency involves the application of a magnetic field that induces a specific change in the proton resonance frequency. This change is caused by the interaction between the magnetic field and the electron spins in the system, resulting in a measurable shift that can be used to determine the temperature. By combining the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency shift with the magnetic field-induced shift, the method can achieve a higher level of precision and reliability. This new approach has been successfully tested in a range of conditions, including temperatures as low as 1.8 K and as high as 300 K. The results demonstrate that the method can achieve a temperature precision of up to 0.1 K, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications.

In the vicinity of a superconducting phase transition, fluctuations in the superconducting order parameter are significantly influenced by material imperfections and random disorder. These factors can be effectively modeled using a renormalization group approach, which utilizes the Ginzburg number to determine the range of temperatures at which such effects become prominent. This theoretical framework is applied to the study of a two-dimensional superconductor with random impurities, where the order parameter is complex and exhibits mean-field behavior at the upper critical dimension. This particular scenario is relevant to the study of superconducting materials such as MgB2 and FeSe, which exhibit superconductivity at two-dimensional dimensions.

This study examines the energy efficiency and reliability of indoor location tracking using a UWB system, focusing on the impact of different IEEE 802.15.4 UWB configurations on energy consumption and signal quality. A comprehensive analysis of 16 UWB channel settings was conducted, revealing a significant variation in energy usage and signal stability. A new framework was developed to optimize the selection of UWB channel settings, balancing energy efficiency and localization accuracy. The proposed approach was tested in a real-world scenario, achieving a 20% reduction in energy consumption and a 20% decrease in localization errors.

We investigate the $k$-median clustering problem for a set of finite points in the Euclidean space, given the distances defined by the $p$-norm. We develop a new algorithm that can solve this problem in fixed-parameter linear time when the parameters $k$, $p$, and the maximum weight $W$ are constant. This is the first known algorithm to achieve fixed-parameter linear time for the $p$-norm $k$-median problem. Our approach relies on a new technique for approximating the $p$-norm, which is of independent interest. We also show that for the $p$-norm $k$-median problem, we can achieve fixed-parameter linear time when the parameters $k$ and $p$ are constant and the maximum weight $W$ is not necessarily constant.

This paper presents a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that combines Q-learning and consensus mechanisms. A new double averaging approach is proposed to ensure the convergence of the method, offering a more comprehensive understanding of its behavior. Unlike existing algorithms, this method converges to the true optimal Q-value rather than a statistical approximation, and also achieves faster convergence rates. A new consensus mechanism is introduced to enhance performance in environments with changing dynamics. A stochastic approximation analysis is conducted to rigorously evaluate the method's convergence properties.

We introduce a coalgebraic extension of the $\nu$-calculus, which generalizes the modal $\mu$-calculus, and is applicable to any functor, including those that allow unguarded variables. This enables our system to handle formulas without guard conditions, and is based on a set of natural coalgebraic rules. These include fixpoint induction, substitution, and a coalgebraic version of the bisimulation reduction rule. We prove that our system is decidable and complete with respect to model checking bisimilarity.

In the context of identifying heat sources within a three-dimensional domain, we utilize a hierarchical Bayesian model, particularly beneficial when dealing with a large number of sources. We examine the application of this model to a specific scenario, the three-dimensional heat equation, and employ a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to explore its posterior distribution. A key aspect of our approach involves utilizing a variational multiscale finite element discretization to handle the high-dimensional nature of the problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by presenting numerical results that showcase its performance.

Estimating air quality at the street level is a complex task due to the significant variation in pollutant concentrations across different areas. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a method for predicting air quality using vehicle sensor data. However, existing approaches often overlook the impact of vehicle paths on data accuracy, leading to inaccurate results. To address this issue, a new method is proposed that considers both vehicle paths and air quality data to impute missing values. By analyzing the relationship between vehicle paths and air quality data, this method can identify and utilize relevant data points to fill in missing values. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The structure of a unitary group linked to $\slf(2, A_n)$ is analyzed in relation to its linear representation theory.

The incorporation of music in videos has become a standard feature, particularly in persuasive videos, as it enhances the overall viewer experience. This research introduces a novel approach to generating background music tailored to the content of a video. The proposed system relies on a deep learning model, which is trained on a dataset of 10,000 YouTube music videos. The model is comprised of two neural networks, each responsible for generating the rhythm and melody components of the music. The system's performance is evaluated using a set of metrics, including the accuracy of beat detection and pitch recognition, as well as the quality of harmony and rhythmic structure. The results indicate that the proposed system achieves high scores in these metrics, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality background music for videos.

A comprehensive analysis of a one-dimensional ion confined within a harmonic trap and influenced by a linearly increasing electric field is presented. The trap's fundamental properties, including its frequency and mass, are considered, and the electric field is modeled as a step function. The classical motion of the ion is described by a Hamiltonian function, and the corresponding quantum operator is derived from it. The energy of the system is determined by calculating the expectation value of the quantum Hamiltonian, and the corresponding classical energy is also calculated. The relationship between the quantum and classical energies is explored, and the corresponding classical position and velocity are derived. The corresponding quantum position and velocity operators are derived from the corresponding classical quantities, and the corresponding quantum operators are derived from the corresponding quantum Hamiltonian. The corresponding quantum operators are derived from the corresponding quantum Hamiltonian, and the corresponding quantum operators are derived from the corresponding quantum Hamiltonian.

Neuroscience models are often under-specified, making it challenging to pinpoint the relevant areas within their parameter space. This limitation restricts their practical application in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that utilizes Bayesian methods to identify the prior distribution of parameters within these models. By doing so, we can determine the areas within the parameter space that are consistent with experimental data. This method is demonstrated using the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, a widely used framework in neuroscience research.

This study tackles the challenge of instance segmentation in scenarios where object classes are unknown, by proposing a novel camouflage fusion learning (CFL) framework. By utilizing a camouflage strategy, the proposed framework enables the segmentation model to adapt to unseen objects without requiring prior class information. In the training process, the model is taught to recognize objects based on their visual similarity to known classes, while maintaining the ability to segment novel objects. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the CFL framework, showcasing its ability to achieve competitive performance on standard benchmarks while effectively handling novel objects.

The article investigates the influence of Lorentz-violating effects on superconductivity within the framework of the Standard Model Extension. It is demonstrated that these effects can significantly affect the Higgs field, leading to the emergence of new types of superconductivity. Specifically, we examine the impact of Lorentz-violating tensors on the coherence length, critical temperature, and energy gap, revealing that these effects can be as substantial as the traditional coherence length, critical temperature, and energy gap.

In the context of AI, we introduce a novel approach to dynamically identify and target specific groups of individuals for data collection, with the ultimate goal of improving model performance. By leveraging group fairness constraints, we utilize existing AI models to predict which groups are most likely to be underrepresented, with the ultimate aim of enhancing overall model performance. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in identifying and targeting groups that are most in need of additional data. Furthermore, we show that our approach can lead to improved model performance while also ensuring that the model adheres to group fairness constraints.

In the context of object detection, the effectiveness of a detector is heavily reliant on the quality of its training data. To improve detector performance, researchers have been focusing on refining the training dataset. This research paper introduces a novel method called R(Det)2, which aims to enhance detector training by refining the training data. R(Det)2 achieves this by employing a data-driven approach to identify and discard low-quality annotations, thereby improving detector performance. The proposed method is evaluated on the widely-used COCO dataset, where it demonstrates a significant improvement in detector performance, surpassing the current state-of-the-art results.

The effectiveness of the FGSM attack in the context of adversarial training is examined, where it is found that simply masking small input gradients does not significantly impact the attack's success. However, when these small gradients are replaced with a uniform value, the attack is notably weakened. This research also investigates the influence of the attack direction's magnitude on the attack's performance and reveals that the optimal magnitude is not always the maximum possible value.

Recent research on primordial black holes has led to the idea that they might be able to make up all of the dark matter.  However, the fact that they have not been detected yet means that scientists must be very careful about how much of the universe's mass they can account for.  In this paper, we examine the effect of a particular spacetime metric on the number of primordial black holes that form.  The metric in question is used to describe the universe's early stages, and it is used to calculate the number of black holes that form.  The results show that the number of black holes that form is not significantly different from what is expected, and that the constraints on the number of black holes that form are still valid.  The reason for this is that the number of black holes that form is not significantly affected by the universe's early expansion.  The results also show that the number of primordial black holes that form is not significantly different from what is expected, and that the constraints on the number of black holes that form are still valid.

This paper presents a new approach to solving complex optimization problems with coupled constraints by leveraging the principles of distributed averaging and time-varying systems. The proposed method involves iteratively updating estimates of Lagrange multipliers and primal variables, which are then used to solve the original optimization problem. The convergence of this algorithm is proven to be stable under certain conditions, including the presence of a "average dwell time" switching signal. The method is also shown to be applicable to a broader class of optimization problems, including those with time-varying constraints.

Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables private computation on untrusted hardware, but its computational efficiency is hindered by the high overhead of CPU-based FHE execution. To address this, we developed BTS, a reconfigurable architecture that accelerates FHE computations. By leveraging arithmetic-logic duality and a novel reconfigurable memory system, BTS can efficiently execute computations while maintaining data confidentiality. Our evaluation of BTS using a suite of benchmarks shows that it outperforms the best existing CPU-based FHE implementation by 1.2x to 10.2x, while also achieving significant speedup over other FHE architectures.

We examine the spectral correlation function of a random matrix ensemble consisting of the sum of two independent circular orthogonal ensemble matrices, each of size N. This function is defined as the expected value of a specific two-point correlation between matrix eigenvalues. We find that it can be expressed as a product of two Jacobi polynomials, specifically $P_n^{(-1,N-N/2)(-1-N/2,N/2-1)}(x)$ and $P_n^{(-1,N-N/2)N-N/2-1,N-N/2-1}(x)$. We then calculate the large N limit of these polynomials and demonstrate that the resulting spectral correlation function is a product of two squared Jacobi polynomials, specifically $P_n^{(-1,-1/2)}(x)$ and $P_n^{(-1,-1)}(1-x)$. We find that the large N limit of the second polynomial is proportional to the Jacobi polynomial $P_{n/2}^{(-1,-1)}(x)$ when n is even, and zero when n is odd. We then show that our results are consistent with a known formula for the spectral correlation function of two independent circular orthogonal ensemble matrices, as derived by Forrester.

Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond are a promising resource for the manipulation and storage of quantum information, but their scalability has been hindered by the difficulty of fabricating them in precise locations. Researchers have recently made significant progress in this area by developing a method to create multiple NV centers in a diamond nanocrystal using a precise fabrication technique. The new method involves growing a nanocrystal with a single NV center, then using a focused laser to introduce additional NV centers at specific locations. The result is a nanocrystal with multiple NV centers that can be used to perform complex quantum information tasks. The researchers have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach by creating a nanocrystal with three NV centers and using it to perform a quantum algorithm. The new method has the potential to revolutionize the way we use NV centers in quantum information tasks, paving the way for a new generation of quantum technologies.

Bell's work in 1986 and 1987 has led to a widespread understanding that local causality alone is insufficient to derive factorization of joint probabilities. This understanding has been largely accepted, yet it has been shown that factorization can indeed be derived from local causality, provided one incorporates a memory assumption. This assumption, which essentially means that the system's state is determined solely by its past, has been underappreciated. When factorization is assumed, one can then deduce that local causality implies an independence principle, which dictates that past events are independent of future events. This independence principle, in turn, has been shown to be equivalent to the assumption of factorization.

We introduce a groundbreaking approach to generating videos that involves continuous motion representation. By utilizing object positions as a form of continuous representation, our method simplifies the task of video generation. We apply this concept to the task of animating static characters, where we track the position of a character's body parts in a single image. By predicting these positions frame by frame, we can create smooth and coherent video sequences. We have developed a novel transformer-based model that can effectively predict object positions. We have also introduced a new loss function to improve the temporal coherence of our results. We have tested our method on multiple datasets and observed that it outperforms existing methods in terms of visual quality and temporal coherence. We have also conducted a comprehensive ablation study to understand the impact of different components of our method.

A key result in representation theory, known as the $\mathbf{\zeta}$-correspondence, draws a connection between the degrees of irreducible characters of a finite group and its subgroup. This correspondence can be visualized as a function that maps degree sets of irreducible characters of a subgroup to degree sets of irreducible characters of the entire group. This paper aims to explore the properties of the $\mathbf{\zeta}$-correspondence function, specifically focusing on its injectivity and its behavior when applied to degree sets of irreducible characters.

This study introduces a novel approach to quantify radiation doses and arrival times using deep learning techniques. The method involves using convolutional neural networks to analyze gamma-ray spectra obtained from a pixelated cadmium-zinc-telluride detector. The proposed model was trained using simulated data and tested on actual measurements from a $^{137}$Cs and $^{131}$I source, achieving an accuracy of 0.5% in dose estimation and 1.5% in date estimation. The method was further tested on gamma-ray spectra from a pixelated CZT detector and demonstrated its potential for accurate dose and date estimation. The results show that this approach can be used to accurately estimate the source of radiation, which is critical for identifying potential nuclear events.

This paper's primary objective is to demonstrate how the results from [1] regarding the compactness of Sobolev spaces with variable exponents on metric measure spaces can be generalized to the case of variable exponents p(x) defined on the metric measure space itself, rather than just remaining constant as previously assumed in [1].

The modulation transfer function (MTF) is a widely used measure of detector performance, but its interpretation can be ambiguous, particularly when considering the MTF of a detector in relation to the MTF of an optical system. This ambiguity arises because the MTF is not a well-defined concept for detectors, but rather a mathematical construct that can be interpreted in multiple ways. This paper aims to clarify the physical meaning of the MTF by deriving it from the optical transfer function and the detector's point spread function, and then deriving an expression for the MTF of an optical system coupled with a pixelated detector. The analysis reveals that the MTF of a detector is not a property of the detector itself, but rather a measure of the combined performance of the detector and the optical system. The paper also discusses the implications of this result for the design of imaging systems, and the importance of considering the effects of the detector on the overall MTF of the system.

Recent research has introduced explanation methods for machine learning models, such as LIME, to help users understand how these models make decisions. However, LIME has limitations, including the need for expert knowledge and the inability to provide a global understanding of the model. To address these issues, we developed a S-LIME approach that uses an SLM to generate explanations for complex ML models, allowing for more accurate and user-friendly explanations. Additionally, our approach enables users to obtain a broader understanding of the model by analyzing the SLM's weights. We tested our method using a real-world dataset, and the results showed that S-LIME produces more accurate and user-friendly explanations compared to LIME, and that users can also gain a better understanding of the model's decision-making process.

We introduce a probabilistic approach to integrating human feedback into a Bayesian convolutional neural network, allowing it to learn from its mistakes. By incorporating feedback into the loss function, the model is updated with the correct labels, and the uncertainty in the predictions is used to determine the extent of this correction. This method enables the model to learn from its errors, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a custom dataset, showing that it outperforms standard training methods.

Our study of Ce$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$'s magnetic properties using inelastic neutron scattering reveals that the low-energy crystal-field levels are the primary source of magnetic fluctuations in the spin-liquid state, as observed in specific heat measurements. The data collected at 10 K shows that the magnetic excitations are localized and follow a specific pattern, which is consistent with the presence of a crystal-field doublet ground state. The observed magnetic excitations are consistent with the crystal-field levels predicted by the $D_{2d}$ point symmetry of the Ce$^{3+}$ ion. The data collected at 10 K also shows that the magnetic excitations are localized and follow a specific pattern, which is consistent with the presence of a crystal-field doublet ground state. The observed magnetic excitations are consistent with the crystal-field levels predicted by the $D_{2d}$ point symmetry of the Ce$^{3+}$ ion.

We demonstrate that the blow-down of a specific type of convex solution in higher-dimensional space approaches a specific geometric shape as a certain parameter tends to infinity. This specific geometric shape is a well-known geometric structure in higher-dimensional geometry. We also establish a uniform limit for a family of convex surfaces in higher-dimensional space under specific conditions as another parameter tends to infinity. Additionally, we prove that a specific geometric structure in higher-dimensional space is unique and has a specific characteristic.

The Weight Fixation mechanism is a training aid that accelerates convergence by locking in the weights of a subset of neurons. It is often overlooked in neural network research, despite its potential to enhance performance. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for characterizing fixation sets in both linear and nonlinear networks. Theorems are provided to identify the optimal set of neurons to fixate, thereby expediting convergence. Additionally, the framework is used to determine the fixed point of the output layer in linear and Hopfield networks. The efficacy of the Weight Fixation mechanism is demonstrated through experiments on the XOR problem, showcasing its ability to expedite training and improve accuracy.

DeepCluE is a novel image clustering method that leverages contrastive learning at both the instance and cluster levels. Unlike traditional methods, it doesn't rely on pre-defined labels, instead utilizing a similarity metric to identify clusters. The algorithm employs a similarity matrix to learn a representation space where images from the same cluster are grouped together. To achieve this, it uses contrastive learning techniques, including instance-level and cluster-level learning, and incorporates a graph-based clustering method to derive a similarity matrix from image features. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, where it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

The increasing interconnectedness of the world has led to a pressing need for effective risk management, as global operations can have far-reaching consequences. To address this challenge, we propose a system that utilizes automated information extraction and analysis to assess risk and inform decision-making processes.

The traditional weighted k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) method has been modified to incorporate the principles of the Topological Data Analysis (TDABC) method. By employing the concept of persistence diagrams, which are generated from a signed distance matrix of k-NN, the TDABC method is able to learn from both the local and global characteristics of the training data. This approach has been found to outperform the k-NN method in handling imbalanced datasets, as well as to be more robust against noisy data. Furthermore, the proposed TDABC method is able to achieve comparable results to the k-NN method when dealing with balanced datasets.

The concept of contrasimilarity, which is derived from contrarelationism, is a similarity concept that arises from the dual relationship with bisimilarity. We utilize this duality to develop a method for verifying process equivalence in regular processes. This involves using contrasimilarity as a refinement criterion, ensuring that two regular processes are equivalent if and only if they exhibit the same contrasimilarity relation as bisimilarity.
